name: Embedded & IoT Engineer
tagline: Build the firmware, hardware and cloud links behind connected devices.
description: For programmers who want to get closer to the hardware, and for electronics hobbyists who want to ship real connected products. You start with the maths, C and computer-systems basics and the electronics every firmware engineer needs, then work up through microcontrollers, peripherals and protocols, RTOS and embedded Linux, wireless and IoT cloud platforms, low-power and PCB design, security, and the testing and debugging practices that get devices into the field and keep them there.
outcomes: Write bare-metal and RTOS firmware in C for a microcontroller, including drivers for I2C, SPI, UART and ADC peripherals
Bring up embedded Linux on a system-on-chip board and write services that run on it
Connect devices over BLE, Wi-Fi, LoRaWAN or cellular and stream data to a cloud IoT platform with MQTT
Design a low-power device from schematic to manufacturable PCB that runs for months on a battery
Secure a device with secure boot, device identity, encrypted communication and safe over-the-air updates
Debug firmware and hardware with JTAG/SWD, logic analysers and oscilloscopes, and automate testing in CI

stages.name: Foundations: maths & programming
stages.description: The maths used in circuits and security, and a solid start in programming: enough to think like a firmware engineer before touching hardware.

items.why: Binary, hex, powers of two and unit prefixes are everyday embedded arithmetic.
Ohm’s law, timer prescalers and battery-life estimates are all algebra.
Geometry background for trigonometry and signals.
Sinusoids describe AC signals, PWM filtering and radio carriers.
Exponentials and logarithms describe RC charging, decibels and battery discharge.
Capacitor and inductor behaviour, energy and average power are calculus.
Rigorous reasoning, needed to follow the number theory behind cryptography.
Modular arithmetic and primes are the maths of RSA, ECC and every security protocol.
Breaking a device’s behaviour into steps and states.
Programming fundamentals in Python, also the language of test scripts and tooling.
Toolchains, flashing utilities and embedded Linux are all driven from the shell.
Structuring programs into functions and modules, the habit good firmware depends on.
Bits, logic, sets and state machines are the discrete maths of firmware.
Ring buffers, queues, linked lists and hash tables are firmware staples.

stages.name: Computing foundations: C, operating systems & networks
stages.description: How computers really work: assembly, C, memory, operating systems, networks and Linux, the ground that every embedded system stands on.

items.why: Registers, memory, assembly and the instruction cycle: the view firmware engineers work from.
C, pointers, memory layout and bit manipulation: the language of embedded systems.
Processes, scheduling, synchronisation and memory management, the concepts behind every RTOS and Linux.
The TCP/IP stack is what IoT devices use to reach the cloud.
Configuring and debugging Linux systems, from your workstation to an embedded board.
HTTP, JSON and web basics behind REST APIs and device dashboards.
Where device telemetry ends up: storing and querying time-series and device data.
Threat models, attacks and defences: the foundation for securing devices.

stages.name: Electronics for embedded engineers
stages.description: The circuits, analog front-ends, digital logic, signals and lab instruments you need to design and debug hardware around a microcontroller.

items.why: Voltage, current and power: the first things to check when a board misbehaves.
Schematics, breadboards and soldering: the maker skills behind every prototype.
Pull-ups, decoupling capacitors and filters are everywhere on an embedded board.
Diodes, transistors and MOSFETs switch loads and protect I/O pins.
Complex numbers and transforms for circuits and signals.
Circuit analysis for sensor front-ends, dividers and RC filters.
Driving relays, motors and LEDs safely from a GPIO pin.
Op-amps amplify and buffer sensor signals before the ADC.
Filtering, amplifying and protecting analog inputs.
Logic gates and Boolean algebra behind every digital interface.
Flip-flops, counters and state machines: the hardware behind timers and serial ports.
Frequency response and sampling theory for anything that measures signals.
Sampling, aliasing and digital filters in firmware.
ADC and DAC resolution, sampling rate and error sources decide measurement quality.
Multimeters, bench supplies and logic analysers on the embedded bench.
The oscilloscope is the firmware engineer’s best friend for timing and signal problems.

stages.name: Microcontrollers & embedded C
stages.description: From blinking an LED to register-level programming: microcontroller architecture, embedded C practice, toolchains and the first debugging skills.

items.why: Your first microcontroller projects: GPIO, sensors and outputs.
C, C++, Rust and MicroPython for embedded work, and when to use each.
Memory maps, interrupts, timers and the embedded development cycle.
AVR, ARM Cortex-M, ESP32, RISC-V: choosing the right MCU for a product.
Pipelines, caches, MPUs and MMUs explain performance and memory protection.
Register-level programming, startup code and interrupt handlers with no OS underneath.
MISRA-style defensive C, volatile, fixed-width types and safe coding patterns.
Stack, heap, static allocation and linker scripts on memory-starved devices.
Reset vectors, bootloaders and startup sequences.
Git for firmware, hardware files and release management.
Make, CMake and vendor build tools for reproducible firmware builds.
Toolchains that compile on your PC and run on the target.
JTAG and SWD let you halt, step and inspect a running microcontroller.
Breakpoints, watchpoints and systematic debugging of firmware.

stages.name: Peripherals, sensors & wired protocols
stages.description: Talking to the outside world: on-chip peripherals, sensors and actuators, and the wired buses that connect chips and boards.

items.why: Timers, PWM, ADC, DMA and watchdogs: the hardware blocks your firmware drives.
UART and RS-485: the simplest and most common device links.
I2C and SPI connect sensors, displays, memories and radios.
1-Wire and similar single-pin buses for low-cost sensors.
USB device classes for configuration, data logging and firmware update.
CAN and LIN, the robust buses used in vehicles and industrial equipment.
Reading real sensors reliably: calibration, filtering and error handling.
Accelerometers and gyros for motion, orientation and wake-on-motion.
Temperature, humidity, pressure and air-quality sensors, the classic IoT inputs.
Motors, relays and solenoids: making devices act, not just sense.
Decoding I2C, SPI and UART traffic with logic analysers when a sensor will not answer.

stages.name: Operating systems: RTOS & embedded Linux
stages.description: Structuring firmware that does many things at once, real-time operating systems for microcontrollers, and embedded Linux for application processors.

items.why: Firmware architecture: layers, state machines, event loops and hardware abstraction.
Interrupts, shared data, mutexes and race conditions in embedded code.
Deadlines, latency, jitter and schedulability: what real-time actually means.
Tasks, schedulers and context switching in an RTOS.
Queues, semaphores, timers and memory pools: the RTOS toolbox.
FreeRTOS, Zephyr and friends: the main RTOS options and how to choose between them.
Writing drivers that separate hardware details from application logic.
Watchdogs, fault handlers and diagnostics so devices recover instead of hanging.
Logging and runtime monitoring on devices with little memory and no screen.
Application-class SoCs such as the Raspberry Pi and i.MX that run embedded Linux.
Bootloaders, kernels, device trees and root filesystems with Yocto and Buildroot.
systemd services, IPC and the user-space side of an embedded Linux device.
Board support packages: bringing an OS up on custom hardware.

stages.name: Connectivity & IoT architecture
stages.description: Getting data off the device: networking, short- and long-range wireless, IoT protocols, and the edge and cloud platforms that manage fleets of devices.

items.why: Ethernet and embedded TCP/IP stacks such as lwIP.
Bluetooth Low Energy, Wi-Fi, Zigbee and Thread: the radios in most IoT devices.
LoRaWAN, Sigfox and NB-IoT for kilometres of range on a coin cell.
LTE-M, NB-IoT and 5G for devices that must connect anywhere.
Mesh networks such as Thread and BLE Mesh extend coverage device by device.
MQTT, CoAP and HTTP: how devices publish telemetry and receive commands.
The device, gateway, network, cloud and application layers of an IoT system.
JSON, CBOR and Protocol Buffers: compact data on constrained links.
REST, gRPC and webhooks that connect device data to applications.
Processing data on gateways and devices to save bandwidth and cut latency.
Cloud services for ingesting, storing and processing device data.
AWS IoT, Azure IoT and similar platforms: device shadows, rules and fleets.
Provisioning, configuring and monitoring thousands of devices in the field.
Bootloaders, A/B partitions and rollback for safe firmware updates.
Staged rollouts, delta updates and fleet-wide OTA without bricking devices.
Metrics, logs and traces from devices in the field.
Time-series storage and pipelines for device data.
Dashboards and analytics that turn telemetry into decisions.

stages.name: Low-power & PCB design
stages.description: Making devices that run for years on a battery and turning a breadboard prototype into a manufacturable printed circuit board.

items.why: Coin cells, Li-ion and LiFePO4: capacity, self-discharge and what they mean for battery life.
LDOs and quiescent current: the power supply choices that make or break battery life.
Power domains, load switches and sequencing on a board.
Sleep modes, clock gating and duty cycling on microcontrollers.
Power budgets, measuring microamps and system-level strategies for multi-year battery life.
From breadboard to perfboard to dev-kit shields: fast hardware iteration.
Clean, reviewable schematics for microcontroller boards.
Placement, grounding, decoupling and routing, including RF keep-outs.
How PCBs are fabricated and assembled.
Designing boards that are cheap and reliable to build in volume.

stages.name: Device security
stages.description: Protecting devices, data and fleets: cryptography, secure boot, identity, secure communication and defending firmware against attack.

items.why: Symmetric and public-key crypto, hashes and signatures, the tools of device security.
Generating, storing and rotating keys on devices that attackers can hold in their hands.
Secure boot and hardware roots of trust so devices only run your firmware.
Certificates and device identity for authenticating to the cloud.
TLS and DTLS on constrained devices.
Memory-safety bugs, hardening and secure coding for firmware.
Firewalls, segmentation and attacks on IoT networks.
Threat modelling and mitigations across the whole device lifecycle.
Tamper resistance, debug-port lockdown and protecting secrets from physical attack.
Handling personal data from sensors and devices responsibly.
Regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act that connected products must meet.

stages.name: Testing, debugging, delivery & electives
stages.description: Shipping devices that work and stay working: hardware debugging, profiling, automated testing and CI, and electives in TinyML, Rust and industrial protocols.

items.why: Tracking down hardware faults with probes, analysers and debug interfaces.
Instruction trace and profiling to find timing and performance problems.
Unit, integration and hardware-in-the-loop testing for firmware.
Test frameworks, mocking hardware and test-driven firmware development.
Static analysis catches the bugs that are hardest to find on target.
Automated builds, tests and releases for firmware.
Production and end-of-line testing so every shipped unit works.
Diagnosing devices you cannot touch, from crash dumps to remote logs.
Elective (Rust/C++ background): objects and interfaces for larger firmware code bases.
Elective: modern C++ and Rust bring memory safety and zero-cost abstractions to firmware.
Elective: Modbus, PROFINET and friends for industrial IoT.
Elective (TinyML background): coordinate geometry needed for multivariable calculus.
Elective (TinyML background): vectors and matrices are the maths of neural networks.
Elective (TinyML background): gradients drive how networks learn.
Elective (TinyML background): what machine learning is and where it fits on devices.
Elective (TinyML background): statistics refresher for machine learning.
Elective (TinyML background): NumPy and notebooks for preparing sensor datasets.
Elective (TinyML background): training, validation and overfitting.
Elective (TinyML background): supervised and unsupervised learning on sensor data.
Elective (TinyML background): the neural networks that TinyML squeezes onto microcontrollers.
Elective: running neural networks on microcontrollers for keyword spotting, gesture and anomaly detection.
